title: Local Privilege Escalation via MSKSSRV Kernel Driver Exploitation
id: 5a8c0d47-1e9f-4b2a-9c3d-1a6e8f2b7c9d
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation of CVE-2024-35250 via local execution of a process that sends crafted IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY request with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag to MSKSSRV kernel driver, indicating potential privilege escalation attempt.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2024/12/cisa-and-fbi-raise-alerts-on-exploited.html
    - https://devco.re/blog/2024/08/23/streaming-vulnerabilities-from-windows-kernel-proxying-to-kernel-part1-en/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1068/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.t1068
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY'
            - 'KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET'
            - 'KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream'
            - 'KsSynchronousIoControlDevice'
        ParentImage|endswith: '\mskssrv.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tools using kernel streaming APIs
    - Debugging or development utilities interacting with kernel drivers
level: high

title: Initial Access via MSKSSRV Kernel Vulnerability Trigger
id: 9f3b7e4a-2c1d-4f5e-8a6b-3c9d1e7f2a8b
status: experimental

references:

author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        CommandLine|contains:

level: high

pipeline.attack_summary: The Slingshot APT uses a complex attack platform involving exploitation of Mikrotik routers through Winbox Loader to download malicious DLLs like ipv4.dll, which then connects to hardcoded IP addresses to download additional components. It employs kernel-mode rootkits (Cahnadr/NDriver) and user-mode modules (GollumApp) for persistence, data exfiltration, and credential access, leveraging known driver vulnerabilities to bypass security controls.

indicators.context: The name appears unencrypted in some of the malicious samples – it is the name of one of the threat actor’s components, so we decided to extend it to the APT as a whole.
The initial loader replaces the victim's legitimate Windows library 'scesrv.dll' with a malicious one of exactly the same size.
One of them – ipv4.dll – has been placed by the APT with what is, in fact, a downloader for other malicious components.

When the target user runs Winbox Loader software (a utility used for Mikrotik router configuration), this connects to the router and downloads some DLLs (dynamic link libraries) from the router’s file system.
Following infection, Slingshot would load a number of modules onto the victim device, including two huge and powerful ones: Cahnadr, the kernel mode module, and GollumApp, a user mode module.
Canhadr, also known as NDriver, contains low-level routines for network, IO operations and so on.

The most sophisticated module is GollumApp. This contains nearly 1,500 user-code functions and provides most of the above described routines for persistence, file system control and C&C communications.
During our research we also found a component called KPWS that turned out to be another downloader for Slingshot components.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.
These vulnerabilities include CVE-2007-5633; CVE-2010-1592, CVE-2009-0824.

We were able to find several cases where the attackers got access to Mikrotik routers and placed a component downloaded by Winbox Loader, a management suite for Mikrotik routers.
I know the Technicolor TC8717T Wireless Telephony DOCSIS 3.0 Modem, 4 Port Router which comes with ISP Xfinity, has been harnessed this attack.

attack_vector.reasoning: The text clearly describes a phishing email with a hyperlink leading to a download link for the malware. The attack vector is straightforward social engineering followed by execution of a downloaded file. While some technical details about anti-analysis techniques are included, they are not part of the initial access mechanism.

pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker uses phishing emails containing links to download a 7z archive with a NetWire RAT variant. The archive contains an executable that performs anti-analysis techniques like mouse movement detection and API breakpoint checking before executing its payload. Once executed, the malware relocates itself, creates registry persistence, collects system information, logs keystrokes, and communicates with a C2 server using DNS resolution to obtain the IP address of the C2 server.

As you can see, the malware file download link is: "hxxps[:]//www[.]mediafire[.]com/file/d86hz5qj21lmhrb/PROFORMA-INVOICE_0990.7z/file".
Its domain is found in the decrypted string, which for this variant is "gbam0001.duckdns[.]org:3366".
Figure 5 is the screenshot of the process tree. You can see the process where NetWire was relocated to "C:\Users\user_name\AppData\Roaming\Install\Host.exe".
NetWire continues to create its home key (HKCU\SOFTWARE\NetWire) as well as adding it into the auto-run group in the victim's registry.
NetWire creates a log folder to store the log files of information that it collects from the victim's system. The log folder is located at "%AppData%\Logs".
It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe).

It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe). If not, it relocates the file into "%AppData%\Install" and renames it as "Host.exe".

Once the connection with its server is established, NetWire starts waiting for the C&C server to reply with a "9B" command packet
1. Obtains a time value how long the victim has been inactive since the last input.Command number: 097h
2. Executes a downloaded executable file or an existing local file like "cmd.exe".Command numbers: 09Ch, 09Ch, 0A3h, 0AFh, 0B6h, 0C3h

3. Performs actions including: exit NetWire process, close the socket to C&C server, read a value from its home key in the system registry, reset or delete a specified registry key, delete the NetWire executable file and relocate its executable file ("Host.exe").Command numbers: 09Fh, 0A0h, 0A1h, 0A2h, 0AEh, 0E5h, 0E7h

5. Steals and collects credentials stored in the victim's system by different software. It focuses on these: 360Chrome, Opera, Mozilla Firefox, Mozilla SeaMonkey, Google Chrome, Comodo Dragon browser, YandexBrowser, Brave-Browser, Mozilla Thunderbird, Microsoft Outlook and Pidgin. It also reads the victim's browser history records from the history folder.Command numbers: 0D4h, 0D5h, 0D6h, 0D7h, 0D8h, 0D9h.

6. Operates the log files in its folder ("%AppData%\Log"), including enumerate log files, get specified log file attribute, read and delete a specified log file.Command numbers: 0CCh, 0CEh, 0CFh, 0D0h.

7. Obtains window handles that are created on the victim's device; sends a windows message to a window by specified windows handle; obtains information of all running processes on the victim's device; kills a running process using a given process ID; obtains a list of TCP or UDP endpoint information (TCP or UDP, local and remote IP address, port, status) as well as the process information (process name, process id) that connects this endpoint.Command numbers: 0BEh, 0C0h, 0C1h, 0C2h, 0E3h.

8. Collects the victim's computer basic information, which include the current username, logon session information, computer name, CPU information, Windows version, memory status, network status, and Windows installation path. It also collects the PowerShell installation path, NetWire executable file full path, and its Log folder full path, etc.Command numbers: 0BAh, 0BCh.

9. Controls the victim's input devices, including the Keyboard and Mouse. By sending keybd_event and mouse_event, it can simulate Keyboard and Mouse operations.Command numbers: 0C5h, 0C6h, 0C7h, 0C8h.
Next, it initializes several global variables and Windows Sockets by calling the API WSAStartup().
Current login User name collected by calling the API GetUserNameA() or from the system environment variable.
Victim's Computer name by calling the API GetComputerNameA().
Victim's Windows version information by calling the API GetVersionExA().
It then calls the _beginthreadex() function to start a thread, the thread function of which registers a window class, whose window procedure function is a keylogger.

It also calls the API ntdll.ZwGetContextThread to obtain the current thread context structure, which contains the CPU debug register status. Once the debugger sets hardware breakpoints, the CPU registers that Dr0, Dr1, Dr2, Dr3, Dr6 and Dr7 are not zero. Register eax is an API address. It checks the address at the beginning to see if they are set to 0CC, 3CD, and 0B0F, which are the opcodes of soft breakpoints (Int 3). Once one of the above conditions is triggered, NetWire goes to a random address to crash itself.
It also calls the API ntdll.ZwGetContextThread to obtain the current thread context structure, which contains the CPU debug register status.

rules_yaml:
title: Initial Access via Malicious SMB Activity and PowerShell Download
id: 52b7a0d3-9f8c-4e6d-b123-456789abcdef
status: experimental
description: Detects initial access via malicious SMB activity against Microsoft Exchange Server, followed by PowerShell command to download a file from a hardcoded internal IP address.
references:
    - https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1190
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_img:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
    selection_cli:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'hxxp://192.168.3.13/email.jpeg'
            - 'New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile'
    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using similar patterns
level: high

title: Execution of PowerShell Script with Bypass Flag
id: 34c8b1e4-0a9d-5f7e-c234-567890bcdef1
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of PowerShell with bypass flag and script file, which is commonly used in credential dumping or deploying malicious payloads.
references:
    - https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_img:
        Image|endswith: '\powershell.exe'
    selection_cli:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-exec bypass -File '
            - '-exec bypass gp.ps1'
            - '-exec bypass -File link.ps1'
    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using PowerShell bypass
level: high

title: Scheduled Task Execution Using Schtasks Command
id: 65d9c2f5-1b0e-6a8f-d345-678901cdef23
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of scheduled tasks using schtasks command, which may be used to run malicious payloads or decoy ransomware.
references:
    - https://symantec-enterprise-blogs.security.com/blogs/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.lateral-movement
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_img:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    selection_cli:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'schtasks /run /tn "\\Microsoft\\Windows\\termsrv\\licensing\\TlsAccess"'
    condition: all of selection_ *
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate scheduled tasks
level: high

title: Credential Dumping Using Rundll32 and Comsvcs.DLL
id: e64219ac-bb54-4ecd-b0c4-605221592a49
status: experimental
description: Detects credential dumping using rundll32 with comsvcs.dll, a known technique used in this attack to extract credentials from memory.

pipeline.attack_summary: An unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2025-59287) exists in Microsoft Windows Server Update Services (WSUS), triggered by unsafe deserialization of SOAP payloads sent to the ReportingWebService endpoint. Attackers exploit this by sending specially crafted requests to default WSUS ports 8530/8531, leading to arbitrary code execution with SYSTEM privileges. The attack chain involves initial access via public exposure of WSUS endpoints, followed by execution through PowerShell commands spawned from wsusservice.exe or w3wp.exe processes, reconnaissance using enumeration commands like whoami and net user /domain, and exfiltration of data to a remote webhook site.

date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1189
    - attack.t1203
    - attack.t1608.004
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_uri:
        cs-uri-query|contains: 'id='
    selection_pattern1:
        cs-uri-query|regex: '\$\([^)]*\)'
    selection_pattern2:

level: high

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with a digitally signed malicious DLL inserted into the SolarWinds Orion Platform via supply chain compromise. The backdoor, Sunburst, executes in the context of SolarWinds.BusinessLayerHost.exe and performs initial reconnaissance before establishing C2 communication using dynamically generated domains. Attackers use techniques like WMI for lateral movement, PowerShell for remote execution, and rundll32 for executing payloads. Raindrop is a secondary loader used to spread laterally across networks, delivering Cobalt Strike payloads with different C2 configurations.

Analysis of the decompiled script shows that the sole purpose of the script is to execute a shellcode that is contained as a hex-encoded string: The screenshot above only shows an excerpt of the complete sequence to create the shellcode string. This string is then decoded to binary data and written to a newly allocated memory area using the BinaryToString and DllStructCreate function calls.

Initial analysis quickly revealed significant similarity to the DarkGate malware, based on the use of a similar initial infection routine (AutoIt scripts) and the observed C2 communication protocol, which matched past analyses of the same malware family.
The AutoIt script is bundled with the.au3file extension which is usually used for plain-text scripts. Instead it contains a pre-compiled script, which would typically use the.a3xextension.

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up describes the malware's behavior post-delivery but does not specify how it initially enters the system; the focus is on post-exploitation capabilities rather than an exploit vector.

pipeline.attack_summary: Kapeka is a novel backdoor used by the Sandworm APT group since at least mid-2022, targeting victims in Eastern Europe. It uses a dropper to install itself on victim machines and then removes itself after execution. The malware collects system information and communicates with threat actors, likely as part of a broader campaign involving GreyEnergy and Prestige ransomware.

indicators.context: The malware, which we are calling "Kapeka", is a flexible backdoor with all the necessary functionalities to serve as an early-stage toolkit for its operators.

The backdoor will first collect information and fingerprint both the machine and user before sending the details on to the threat actor. This allows tasks to be passed back to the machine or the backdoor's configuration to be updated.
WithSecure discovered overlaps between Kapeka, GreyEnergy, and Prestige ransomware attacks which are all reportedly linked to a group known as Sandworm.
It is likely that Kapeka was used in intrusions that led to the deployment of Prestige ransomware in late 2022.

pre_review_rules:
title: macOS Terminal Malicious Copy-Paste Command Execution
id: 5a8d7c9e-2b4f-4c6d-a8e1-3f0a2b5c7d9e
status: experimental
description: Detects initial access via malicious copy-paste commands in macOS Terminal that download and execute install.sh scripts, typically used by AMOS stealer campaigns.
references:
    - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/i/an-mdr-analysis-of-the-amos-stealer-campaign.html
    - https://hunt.io/blog/macos-clickfix-applescript-terminal-phishing
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/004/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/002/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1204.004
    - attack.t1566.002
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: macos
detection:
    selection_cli:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'curl -fsSL hxxps://.*\/get.*\/install\.sh'
    condition: selection_cli
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using curl to download installers
level: high

status: experimental
description: Detects the execution of rundll32.exe following the opening of a macro-enabled Office document, which is a common technique used in phishing campaigns to execute malware.
references:
    - https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/05/tactics-techniques-procedures-associated-with-maze-ransomware-incidents.html
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/

author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1204
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith: '\rundll32.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: 'macro'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate use of rundll32.exe with macro-related parameters
level: high

references:
    - https://www.fireeye.com/blog/threat-research/2020/05/tactics-techniques-procedures-associated-with-maze-ransomware-incidents.html
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-05
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1204
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_img:
        Image|endswith:
            - \WINWORD.exe
            - \EXCEL.EXE
            - \POWERPNT.EXE
    selection_cmdline:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '.docm'
            - '.xlsm'

    condition: all of selection_ *

level: medium

title: Persistence via Creation of Macro File for Outlook

status: experimental
description: Detects the creation of macro files for Outlook, a technique often used to establish persistence after initial compromise.

    - Legitimate macro development or configuration in Outlook
level: high

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up clearly describes the initial infection vector as physical insertion of USB drives with LNK files that trigger autorun behavior. The attack chain is well-defined and focuses on user interaction with removable media rather than network-based exploitation.

pipeline.attack_summary: Raspberry Robin is a worm that initially spreads via infected USB drives containing LNK files disguised as folders. Upon insertion, it leverages autorun.inf and Windows shortcut mechanisms to execute malicious payloads through cmd.exe and msiexec.exe, installing malware from compromised QNAP NAS devices. It uses living-off-the-land binaries (LOLBins) like rundll32.exe, odbcconf.exe, control.exe, and fodhelper.exe for execution and persistence. The malware also employs registry keys such as UserAssist and RunOnce to maintain persistence and evade detection. It has evolved into a distribution platform for other malware families including FakeUpdates, IcedID, Bumblebee, and TrueBot, often leading to hands-on-keyboard attacks and ransomware deployment by groups like DEV-0243 (EvilCorp) and DEV-0950 (FIN11/TA505).

indicators.context: Raspberry Robin's LNK file points to cmd.exe to launch the Windows Installer service msiexec.exe and install a malicious payload.
Raspberry Robin uses msiexec.exe to install a malicious payload hosted on compromised QNAP network attached storage (NAS) devices.
Raspberry Robin spawns additional processes using system binaries such as rundll32.exe to run malicious code.
Raspberry Robin uses odbcconf.exe as a living-off-the-land binary (LOLBins) to run malicious code.
Raspberry Robin uses control.exe as a LOLBin to run malicious code.
Raspberry Robin launches code via fodhelper.exe, a system binary for managing optional features, as a user access control (UAC) bypass.
Raspberry Robin uses regsvr32.exe to launch the portable executable (PE) file, allowing randomized non-standard file extension to launch the executable content.
Upon insertion of the infected drive or launching of the LNK file, the UserAssist registry key in Windows is updated with a new value indicating a program was launched by Windows.
Raspberry Robin persists by adding itself to the RunOnce key of the registry hive associated with the user who executed the initial malware install.
In earlier infections, this file used a generic file name like recovery.lnk.
Some Raspberry Robin drives have a configured autorun.inf which is used to specify which code to start when the drive is plugged in.
